title: Verb Patterns
overview: This unit is about what comes after a verb, and it is the area where a learner's English most often stops sounding like a learner's. Some verbs take to, some take -ing, a few take both with different meanings, and several hundred take a small word that changes what they mean entirely. There is no rule for most of it, which is worth saying plainly — but there are patterns, and there is a way of learning the rest that actually works.
learningPath: Read and listen to the Lesson. There are four patterns.
Open Patterns. Card 1 has no rule and card 3 has no rule — both say so.
Learn the words. Twenty-nine, in five groups.
Read the three texts aloud. The third is a plain-English rewrite of a formal note.
Do the Practice. Practice 2 is the diagnostic — the verbs that take both.
Record yourself using twelve phrasal verbs about your own week.
Take the quiz, then update My progress.
lectureScript:
This unit is about what comes after a verb, and I want to start by being honest about how much of it is learnable by rule. Not much. But the parts that are not learnable by rule are learnable by pattern, and there is a method for the rest.
First pattern: gerund and infinitive after a verb.
Some verbs are followed by to plus the verb. I decided to leave. I hope to finish. I intend to ask.
Some are followed by the -ing form. I enjoy working here. I avoid asking. I finished reading it.
There is no rule that tells you which. It is like the adjective and preposition pairings in Unit 1 of this level — the pattern belongs to the individual verb and it is learned with the verb.
But there are three tendencies that cover a useful proportion.
Verbs about the future — intending, deciding, hoping, planning, agreeing, promising, refusing — tend to take to. That makes sense: to points forward.
Verbs about liking, disliking and continuing tend to take -ing. Enjoy, avoid, mind, risk, keep, finish, practise.
And everything after a preposition takes -ing, always, with no exceptions. Interested in working. Good at explaining. Instead of waiting. Before leaving. That is the one absolutely reliable rule in this area, and it is the same one from Unit 1.
Now the interesting part: a small group of verbs take both, and the two mean different things.
Remember. I remembered to lock the door — I remembered, and then I locked it. I remember locking the door — I locked it, and now I have the memory.
So remember plus to is about the future task. Remember plus -ing is about the past memory.
Stop. I stopped to read the notice — I stopped in order to read it. I stopped reading the notice — I was reading and I stopped.
Try. I tried to open it — I attempted it, probably unsuccessfully. I tried opening it — I opened it as an experiment, to see whether it would help.
Regret. I regret to tell you — I am about to tell you and I am sorry. I regret telling you — I told you and I wish I had not.
Four verbs, and they are worth learning properly, because getting them backwards produces a sentence that means the opposite of what you intended.
Second pattern: -ing forms as subject and object.
An -ing form can be the subject of a sentence, and this is how English talks about activities in general.
Waiting is the worst part. Explaining it takes longer than doing it. Reading the small print would have saved me an hour.
And as the object: I hate waiting. She recommended reading it twice.
One thing to notice, because it catches people. When an -ing form is the subject, the verb is singular. Waiting is the worst part, not waiting are. Even when the -ing phrase is long — checking every pallet before it goes out is slow — the verb stays singular, because the whole phrase is one activity.
Third pattern, and this is the big one: phrasal verbs.
A phrasal verb is a verb plus a small word, and the combination often means something you could not guess from the parts.
Look is straightforward. Look into means investigate. Look after means take care of. Look up means find in a reference. Look out means be careful. One verb, four completely unrelated meanings.
There are several thousand of these and they are the single largest gap between formal English and the English people actually speak. And here is the practical point.
Almost every phrasal verb has a formal one-word equivalent, and the formal one is usually the one learners know.
Look into is investigate. Carry out is perform. Set up is establish. Put off is postpone. Call off is cancel. Sort out is resolve. Come across is encounter. Deal with is handle. Point out is indicate. Bring up is raise. Run out is exhaust.
So you have not been missing the meanings. You have been missing the versions people say.
That is genuinely good news, and it also tells you which to use where. The one-word version belongs in formal writing. The phrasal version belongs in speech and in ordinary writing, and a document written entirely in one-word Latin verbs reads as stiff.
One grammatical thing about them. Some phrasal verbs can be separated and some cannot.
Separable: I put off the meeting, or I put the meeting off. Both fine. And if the object is a pronoun, it must go in the middle — I put it off, never I put off it.
Inseparable: I looked into the problem, never I looked the problem into. And I looked into it, never I looked it into.
There is no reliable way to tell which is which, and the pronoun test is the practical one: try it with a pronoun and see which sounds possible.
Fourth pattern: adjective plus infinitive.
Some adjectives are followed by to plus the verb, and the group is worth having because it is small and very useful.
I am reluctant to agree. She is eager to start. It is easy to say. They are likely to refuse. He is bound to notice. I am liable to forget.
And two structures built on it that appear constantly.
It is plus adjective plus to. It is difficult to explain. It is important to check. This is how English makes a general statement about an activity.
And too and enough, from Level 1 Unit 8, with an infinitive. It is too late to change it. It is not clear enough to act on. Notice that too comes before the adjective and enough comes after.
Go to Patterns.

words.meaning: To take pleasure in something.
words.example: I enjoy working with people who ask questions.
practice: She enjoys explaining things.
I did not enjoy waiting.
Nobody enjoys being corrected.
He enjoys it more than he admits.
words.starter: I enjoy working with people who ask
words.tutor: Enjoy always takes -ing. Say enjoy doing, never enjoy to do.

words.meaning: To do something that might have a bad result.
words.example: I did not want to risk losing the order.
practice: She risked being late.
Do not risk it.
He risked saying what he thought.
It risks making things worse.
words.starter: I did not want to risk losing the
words.tutor: Risk takes -ing. Say risk losing and risk being, twice each.

words.meaning: To feel angry about something you think is unfair.
words.example: She resented being asked twice.
practice: I resent having to explain it again.
Nobody resented the change.
He resents being told what to do.
I do not resent it at all.
words.starter: She resented being asked
words.tutor: Notice resent being asked — a passive -ing form. Say it twice.

words.meaning: To accept something you do not like.
words.example: I can tolerate waiting; I cannot tolerate not being told.
practice: She tolerated it for a year.
Nobody should have to tolerate that.
It tolerates being moved.
I tolerate it rather than accept it.
words.starter: I can tolerate waiting; I cannot tolerate not being
words.tutor: Notice not being told — the negative goes before the -ing form. Say it aloud.

words.meaning: To think seriously about doing something.
words.example: I contemplated leaving and then stayed another year.
practice: She is contemplating applying.
I would not contemplate doing that.
He contemplated it for a week.
Nobody contemplated the alternative.
words.starter: I contemplated leaving and then stayed another
words.tutor: Contemplate is formal and takes -ing. Say contemplate doing something.

words.meaning: To suggest that something is good or should be done.
words.example: She recommended reading it twice.
practice: I would recommend waiting.
He recommended that we postpone it.
Nobody recommended anything.
It comes highly recommended.
words.starter: She recommended reading it
words.tutor: Recommend takes -ing or a that-clause, never to. Say both correct forms.

words.meaning: To plan to do something.
words.example: I intend to ask before the end of the week.
practice: She never intended to stay.
What do you intend to do?
It was not intended to work that way.
I fully intend to finish it.
words.starter: I intend to ask before the end of the
words.tutor: Intend is a future verb, so it takes to. Say intend to do, never intend doing.

words.meaning: To try very hard over time.
words.example: We strive to answer within two days.
practice: She strove to make it work.
They strive to keep costs down.
Striving is not the same as achieving.
We strive to improve.
words.starter: We strive to answer within two
words.tutor: Strive is formal and takes to. Say where you would meet it — usually in policies.

words.meaning: To try to achieve something.
words.example: We aim to reply within a week.
practice: I aim to finish by Friday.
What are you aiming to do?
They aimed to cut costs by a tenth.
Aiming to and promising to are different.
words.starter: We aim to reply within a
words.tutor: Say we aim to and we will. Aim is a softer commitment.

words.meaning: To usually do something, or to be likely to.
words.example: I tend to check twice.
practice: It tends to happen on Fridays.
She tends to be right about this.
Deliveries tend to arrive late.
I tend not to say anything.
words.starter: I tend to check
words.tutor: Tend to is a very useful hedge. Say I tend to think, from Unit 7.

words.meaning: To not succeed in doing something.
words.example: The report fails to say who decided.
practice: She failed to mention it.
It failed to work.
Nobody failed to notice.
The check failed twice.
words.starter: The report fails to say who
words.tutor: Fail to is often a polite way of saying somebody did not do something. Say it about a document.

words.meaning: To have earned something by what you have done.
words.example: She deserves to be told first.
practice: It deserves a proper answer.
Nobody deserves that.
He deserved to hear it from me.
It does not deserve the attention.
words.starter: She deserves to be told
words.tutor: Notice deserves to be told — an infinitive passive. Say it twice.

words.meaning: To do or perform something planned. Formal equivalent: perform.
words.example: The inspection was carried out on Tuesday.
practice: We carried out the checks ourselves.
Nothing has been carried out yet.
Carry it out before Friday.
They carried out two audits.
words.starter: The inspection was carried out on
words.tutor: Say carry out and perform. One is speech, one is a report.

words.meaning: To establish or arrange something new. Formal equivalent: establish.
words.example: They set up a new system in March.
practice: It was set up two years ago.
Can you set it up for Friday?
Nothing has been set up.
Setting it up took a week.
words.starter: They set up a new system in
words.tutor: Set up is separable. Say set it up, never set up it.

words.meaning: To accept work or responsibility; or to employ. Formal equivalent: assume, recruit.
words.example: We took on two new staff in the spring.
practice: She took on far too much.
I would not take that on.
Nobody took it on.
They are taking on more work.
words.starter: We took on two new staff in the
words.tutor: Take on means both accept work and employ people. Say one sentence with each.

words.meaning: To move something to a later time. Formal equivalent: postpone.
words.example: The meeting has been put off until Friday.
practice: They put it off twice.
Do not put it off any longer.
It was put off at short notice.
Putting it off will not help.
words.starter: The meeting has been put off until
words.tutor: Separable, and with a pronoun it must split. Say put it off, never put off it.

words.meaning: To cancel something arranged. Formal equivalent: cancel.
words.example: They called off the visit at the last minute.
practice: It was called off on Thursday.
They called it off.
Nothing was called off.
Do not call it off yet.
words.starter: They called off the visit at the last
words.tutor: Say called it off. The pronoun goes in the middle.

words.meaning: To deal with a problem and put it right. Formal equivalent: resolve.
words.example: It took a fortnight to sort out.
practice: Can you sort it out?
Nothing has been sorted out.
They sorted out the paperwork.
Sorting it out was the easy part.
words.starter: It took a fortnight to sort
words.tutor: Sort out is very common in speech and rare in formal writing. Say the formal equivalent.

words.meaning: To investigate. Formal equivalent: investigate.
words.example: Somebody is looking into it.
practice: We looked into three options.
Nothing was looked into.
I will look into it and let you know.
It is being looked into.
words.starter: Somebody is looking into
words.tutor: Inseparable: look into it, never look it into. Try the pronoun and hear the difference.

words.meaning: To handle a problem or a person. Formal equivalent: handle, address.
words.example: Who deals with complaints here?
practice: It was dealt with the same day.
I will deal with it.
Nothing has been dealt with.
She deals with the suppliers.
words.starter: Who deals with complaints
words.tutor: Inseparable. Say deal with it, never deal it with.

words.meaning: To find or meet by chance. Formal equivalent: encounter.
words.example: I came across it while looking for something else.
practice: Have you come across this before?
I came across two errors.
Nobody came across anything.
She comes across as confident.
words.starter: I came across it while looking for something
words.tutor: Come across also means seem: she comes across as confident. Say both meanings.

words.meaning: To mention a subject. Formal equivalent: raise.
words.example: Nobody brought up the cost.
practice: She brought it up at the meeting.
I would rather not bring it up.
It was brought up twice.
Bringing it up now would not help.
words.starter: Nobody brought up the
words.tutor: Separable. Say brought it up, never brought up it.

words.meaning: To draw attention to a fact. Formal equivalent: indicate, note.
words.example: She pointed out that the figures were old.
practice: Somebody pointed it out.
It is worth pointing out.
Nobody pointed out the error.
As she pointed out.
words.starter: She pointed out that the figures were
words.tutor: Point out is a neutral reporting verb, from Unit 9. Say she pointed out that.

words.meaning: To have none left. Formal equivalent: be exhausted.
words.example: We ran out of the smaller size.
practice: Time is running out.
It has run out.
We never run out.
They ran out halfway through.
words.starter: We ran out of the smaller
words.tutor: Notice run out of something. Say run out and run out of, and hear the difference.

words.meaning: Unwilling and hesitating.
words.example: I am reluctant to agree without seeing it.
practice: She was reluctant to say anything.
He agreed reluctantly.
I am reluctant rather than opposed.
They were reluctant to commit.
words.starter: I am reluctant to agree without seeing
words.tutor: Reluctant takes to plus the verb. Say I am reluctant to, then give a reason.

words.meaning: Very keen to do something.
words.example: She was eager to start.
practice: I am eager to hear what they say.
Nobody seemed eager.
He was eager to help.
Eager rather than merely willing.
words.starter: She was eager to
words.tutor: Say eager to and keen to, from Unit 1. Both take an infinitive.

words.meaning: Certain to happen or to do something.
words.example: Somebody is bound to notice.
practice: It is bound to happen eventually.
She is bound to ask.
That was bound to go wrong.
It is bound to be expensive.
words.starter: Somebody is bound to
words.tutor: Bound to means certain to. Say it about something you expect.

words.meaning: Likely to do something, often something unwanted.
words.example: I am liable to forget if nobody reminds me.
practice: The old machines are liable to fail.
It is liable to change.
You are liable to be asked.
Liable to and likely to are close.
words.starter: I am liable to forget if nobody reminds
words.tutor: Liable to usually carries something unwanted. Say liable to and likely to.

words.meaning: Tending to suffer from or do something bad.
words.example: That bay is prone to flooding.
practice: He is prone to exaggerate.
The system is prone to failure.
Prone to error rather than careless.
It is prone to happen in winter.
words.starter: That bay is prone to
words.tutor: Notice prone to takes a noun or -ing as well as an infinitive. Say prone to flooding and prone to fail.

readings.title: The Four Verbs That Reverse
readings.passage:
Most verbs take either to or -ing after them, and which one has to be learned with the verb. There are tendencies — future verbs like intend, decide and hope take to; liking and continuing verbs like enjoy, avoid and finish take -ing — and one absolute rule, which is that anything after a preposition takes -ing.
But there is a small group that takes both, and the two mean different things. These four are worth learning properly, because getting them the wrong way round produces a sentence that means the opposite of what you intended.
Remember.
I remembered to lock the door. First I remembered, then I locked it. The locking happened.
I remember locking the door. First I locked it, and now I have the memory. Also true, but it is describing a memory rather than a task.
So remember plus to points forward to a task. Remember plus -ing points back to a memory.
Stop.
I stopped to read the notice. I stopped walking in order to read it.
I stopped reading the notice. I was reading and I stopped.
Those describe opposite actions. In the first you started reading; in the second you finished.
Try.
I tried to open it. I attempted it, and the sentence usually implies I failed.
I tried opening it. I opened it as an experiment, to see whether that would solve the problem.
So try plus to is an attempt at something difficult. Try plus -ing is an experiment with something easy.
Regret.
I regret to tell you that your application has been unsuccessful. I am about to tell you, and I am sorry.
I regret telling you. I told you, and I wish I had not.
The first is a formal opening for bad news. The second is an admission.
Four verbs, eight sentences. They repay being learned as pairs rather than one at a time, because it is the contrast that makes each one stick.

readings.title: You Already Know the Meanings
readings.passage:
Phrasal verbs are usually described as the hardest part of English vocabulary, and there is a reframing that makes them much less daunting.
Almost every common phrasal verb has a formal one-word equivalent — and the one-word version is usually the one learners already know.
Look into is investigate.
Carry out is perform.
Set up is establish.
Put off is postpone.
Call off is cancel.
Sort out is resolve.
Come across is encounter.
Deal with is handle.
Bring up is raise.
Point out is indicate.
Run out is exhaust.
Take on is assume, or recruit.
So you have not been missing the concepts. You have been missing the versions people actually say, and that is a much smaller problem.
It also tells you which to use where, which most word lists do not.
The one-word Latin verbs belong in formal writing — reports, policies, official letters. The phrasal versions belong in speech and in ordinary writing.
A document written entirely in one-word verbs reads as stiff and slightly evasive. A report that says we shall endeavour to ascertain the cause is saying we will find out what happened, and the second version is not less professional. It is clearer.
The reverse is also a mistake. Sort out and deal with in a formal complaint sound casual where resolve and address would not.
Then there is the grammatical question, which is genuinely awkward. Some phrasal verbs can be split by their object and some cannot.
Separable: I put off the meeting, or I put the meeting off. Both correct.
Inseparable: I looked into the problem. I looked the problem into is not English.
There is no reliable way to tell which is which by looking at them. The practical test uses a pronoun, because pronouns behave more strictly than nouns.
With a separable verb, a pronoun object must go in the middle. I put it off. I put off it is wrong.
With an inseparable verb, the pronoun stays after the whole thing. I looked into it. I looked it into is wrong.
So: try it with a pronoun. Whichever position sounds possible is the one the verb allows, and that single test resolves most cases.

readings.documentType: A formal note and its plain rewrite
readings.title: The Same Message, Two Registers
readings.setting: A note circulated to staff, and the version the supervisor sent afterwards because nobody had understood the first one.
readings.passage:
ORIGINAL NOTE

  Following the incident of 14 March,
  management has resolved to postpone the
  implementation of the revised loading
  procedure until an investigation has
  been concluded.

  An inspection will be performed during
  the week commencing 21 March.
  Personnel are requested to refrain from
  utilising Bay 2 pending the outcome.

  Any anomalies encountered should be
  indicated to a supervisor without delay.

  Management regrets to advise that the
  training scheduled for 24 March has
  been cancelled. A revised date will be
  scheduled once the investigation has
  concluded.

-----------------------------------------

  WHAT THE SUPERVISOR SENT

  After what happened on 14 March, we're
  putting off the new loading procedure
  until somebody has looked into it
  properly.

  There'll be an inspection the week of
  the 21st. Please don't use Bay 2 until
  we know more.

  If you come across anything odd, point
  it out to a supervisor straight away -
  don't wait.

  Sorry, but the training on the 24th has
  been called off. We'll set up another
  date once the inspection is done.

comprehension.q: What is the difference between I remembered to lock the door and I remember locking the door?
comprehension.a: The first means you remembered and then locked it — a task completed. The second means you locked it and now have the memory.
comprehension.why: Remember plus to points forward to a task; remember plus -ing points back to a memory. Reversing them describes a different event.

comprehension.q: Why does the text say I stopped to read and I stopped reading describe opposite actions?
comprehension.a: In the first you stopped doing something else in order to start reading. In the second you were reading and you finished.
comprehension.why: It is the clearest of the four pairs, because one sentence starts the reading and the other ends it.

comprehension.q: What is the one absolute rule in this area?
comprehension.a: Anything after a preposition takes -ing. Interested in working, good at explaining, instead of waiting, before leaving.
comprehension.why: It is the same rule as in Unit 1 of this level and it has no exceptions, which makes it worth more than any of the tendencies.

comprehension.q: What is the reframing the text offers for phrasal verbs?
comprehension.a: Almost every common phrasal verb has a formal one-word equivalent, and the one-word version is usually the one learners already know.
comprehension.why: It converts a vocabulary problem into a register problem, which is a much smaller one.

comprehension.a: The one-word Latin verbs belong in formal writing; the phrasal versions belong in speech and ordinary writing.
comprehension.why: Learners often assume the formal version is always safer. A document written entirely in one-word verbs reads as stiff and slightly evasive.

comprehension.q: What is the pronoun test, and what does it decide?
comprehension.a: Try the verb with a pronoun object. With a separable verb the pronoun must go in the middle — I put it off. With an inseparable one it stays after the whole verb — I looked into it. Whichever sounds possible is the pattern the verb allows.
comprehension.why: There is no way to tell separable from inseparable by looking, and this single test resolves most cases.

comprehension.q: Find four phrasal verbs in the supervisor's version and give the formal equivalent used in the original note.
comprehension.a: Putting off for postpone, looked into for investigation, come across for encountered, point out for indicated, called off for cancelled, set up for schedule. Any four.
comprehension.why: The two documents say the same thing in two registers, so every phrasal verb has its formal twin visible a few lines above.

comprehension.q: The original says management regrets to advise. What does regret plus to mean here?
comprehension.a: That management is about to give bad news and is sorry to be giving it — not that it regrets having given it.
comprehension.why: It is the formal use of regret plus infinitive from Reading 1, appearing in exactly the context that produces it.

comprehension.q: Which version is clearer, and does clearer mean less professional?
comprehension.a: The supervisor's version is clearer, and it is not less professional. It says the same things and leaves nothing out, and it was written because nobody had understood the first one.
comprehension.why: The judgement matters because learners assume formality equals competence. The original failed at the only job it had.

comprehension.q: Is there anything the original does that the supervisor's version does not?
comprehension.a: It is more precise about two things: pending the outcome is tighter than until we know more, and the week commencing 21 March is unambiguous where the week of the 21st is slightly less so.
comprehension.why: The honest answer is not that formal writing is worse. Some of its vocabulary is genuinely more precise, and noticing which parts is the harder half of the reading.

grammar.title: To or -ing after a verb
grammar.explanation: There is no rule that tells you which. It is learned with the verb, like the prepositions in Unit 1. What there is instead is three tendencies and one absolute rule.
grammar.rule:
NO RULE. LEARNED WITH THE VERB.

THREE TENDENCIES
  future verbs -> TO
     intend, decide, hope, plan, agree,
     promise, refuse, aim, offer
  liking / continuing -> -ING
     enjoy, avoid, mind, risk, keep,
     finish, practise, tolerate
  after a PREPOSITION -> always -ING
     interested in working
     good at explaining
     instead of waiting
  ^ this one has NO exceptions.

FOUR VERBS TAKE BOTH, DIFFERENTLY

  REMEMBER
     to lock  = the task, done
     locking  = the memory
  STOP
     to read  = stopped in order to read
     reading  = was reading, and stopped
  TRY
     to open  = attempted, often failed
     opening  = experimented
  REGRET
     to tell  = about to give bad news
     telling  = wish I had not

  Getting these backwards means the
  OPPOSITE of what you intended.
grammar.workedExample:
You want to say you did not forget to lock the door, and that you did lock it.
1. Is this about a task you carried out, or about a memory you have?
2. A task. So remember takes to.
3. Result: I remembered to lock the door.
4. Check the alternative: I remember locking the door. That says you have a memory of doing it — which is a claim about your memory rather than about the door.
Now one where the tendency does the work. You want to say you avoid something.
1. Avoid is a liking-and-continuing verb, so it takes -ing.
2. Result: I avoid asking unless I have to.
And the absolute rule. You want to say you are interested in a job.
1. Interested takes the preposition in.
2. Anything after a preposition takes -ing, with no exceptions.
3. Result: I am interested in working here — never interested in to work.
grammar.mistake: Putting a plain infinitive after a preposition — interested in to work, good at to explain. That is the one rule with no exceptions, so it is the first thing to fix. The other error is reversing one of the four both-verbs, which does not produce a wrong sentence but produces a different one: I stopped to read and I stopped reading describe opposite actions.
grammar.tip: After a preposition, always -ing. The four both-verbs are learned as pairs.
grammar.practice:
Write to or -ing.
1. I intend ____ (ask) before Friday.
2. I enjoy ____ (work) with people who ask questions.
3. I am interested in ____ (work) here.
4. I remembered ____ (lock) the door. (and you locked it)
5. I remember ____ (lock) the door. (you have the memory)
6. I stopped ____ (read) the notice. (you were walking, then read it)
7. I stopped ____ (read) the notice. (you were reading, then stopped)
8. I regret ____ (tell) you that it has been cancelled.
grammar.answers:
1. to ask  2. working  3. working  4. to lock  5. locking  6. to read  7. reading  8. to tell
Number 3 is the absolute rule — after the preposition in, nothing but -ing is possible.
Numbers 4 and 5 are the same words with opposite orientations: a task done, and a memory held.
Numbers 6 and 7 describe opposite actions. In 6 you started reading; in 7 you finished.
Number 8 is the formal bad-news opening. I regret telling you would mean you wished you had not said it.

grammar.title: -ing forms as subject and object
grammar.explanation: An -ing form can be the subject of a sentence, which is how English talks about an activity in general. There is one agreement rule that catches almost everybody.
grammar.rule:
AS SUBJECT
  Waiting is the worst part.
  Explaining it takes longer than doing it.
  Reading the small print would have
     saved me an hour.

AS OBJECT
  I hate waiting.
  She recommended reading it twice.

THE AGREEMENT RULE
  an -ing subject is SINGULAR.

  Waiting IS the worst part.   not are
  Checking every pallet before it goes
     out IS slow.
  ^ long phrase, still singular. The
    whole thing is ONE activity.

THE NEGATIVE GOES BEFORE IT
  Not being told was the problem.
  I resent not being asked.

PASSIVE -ING EXISTS TOO
  being asked, being told, being moved
     She resented being asked twice.

COMPARE WITH THE INFINITIVE SUBJECT
  To wait is the worst part.
  ^ grammatical, and much rarer.
    English prefers the -ing form here.
grammar.workedExample:
You want to say that the waiting is the hardest part of a process.
1. The subject is an activity, not a thing, so use an -ing form: waiting.
2. Put it at the front: Waiting…
3. Now the verb. An -ing subject is singular, always.
4. Result: Waiting is the worst part.
Now a longer one. You want to say that checking every pallet before dispatch is slow.
1. The whole activity is the subject: checking every pallet before it goes out.
2. That is nine words and it is still one activity, so the verb stays singular.
3. Result: Checking every pallet before it goes out is slow.
4. The temptation is to write are, because pallets is plural and sits close to the verb. That is the error the rule exists to prevent.
And the negative: Not being told was the problem. Not goes in front of the -ing form, not inside it.
grammar.mistake: Making the verb plural because a plural noun sits inside the -ing phrase — checking every pallet before it goes out are slow. The subject is the activity, not the pallets. The other error is putting the negative in the wrong place: being not told rather than not being told.
grammar.tip: An -ing subject is one activity, so the verb is singular.
grammar.practice:
Write the sentence with an -ing subject or object.
1. The waiting is the worst part.
2. It takes longer to explain it than to do it.
3. Checking every pallet before dispatch — say it is slow.
4. You were not told, and that was the problem.
5. She was asked twice, and she resented it.
6. She suggested you read it twice.
grammar.answers:
1. Waiting is the worst part.
2. Explaining it takes longer than doing it.
3. Checking every pallet before it goes out is slow.
4. Not being told was the problem.
5. She resented being asked twice.
6. She recommended reading it twice.
Every verb after an -ing subject is singular — is, takes, is, was. In number 3 the plural pallets sits right next to the verb and the verb still stays singular.
Numbers 4 and 5 use passive -ing forms: being told and being asked. In 4 the negative goes before the whole thing.
Number 6 has the -ing form as an object, after recommend, which never takes to.

grammar.title: Phrasal verbs
grammar.explanation: A verb plus a small word, often meaning something you could not guess. There are thousands, and the useful news is that you already know most of the meanings under their formal names.
grammar.rule:
ONE VERB, SEVERAL MEANINGS
  look into  = investigate
  look after = take care of
  look up    = find in a reference
  look out   = be careful

YOU ALREADY KNOW THE MEANINGS
  look into  -> investigate
  carry out  -> perform
  set up     -> establish
  put off    -> postpone
  call off   -> cancel
  sort out   -> resolve
  come across-> encounter
  deal with  -> handle
  bring up   -> raise
  point out  -> indicate

REGISTER
  one-word Latin verbs -> formal writing
  phrasal verbs -> speech and ordinary
     writing

SEPARABLE OR NOT
  separable:   put off the meeting
               put the meeting off
  inseparable: look into the problem
               (never look the problem into)

THE PRONOUN TEST
  separable   -> pronoun in the MIDDLE
     put it off      (not put off it)
  inseparable -> pronoun AFTER
     look into it    (not look it into)
grammar.workedExample:
You want to say the meeting has been moved to a later date, in an ordinary message to colleagues.
1. The formal verb is postpone. The phrasal equivalent is put off.
2. Which register? An ordinary message to colleagues, so the phrasal version.
3. Result: We have put the meeting off until Friday. Or: We have put off the meeting until Friday. Both work, because put off is separable.
4. Now with a pronoun: We have put it off. Never we have put off it — with a separable verb, a pronoun must go in the middle.
Now an inseparable one. Somebody is investigating a problem.
1. Look into is the phrasal equivalent of investigate.
2. Try the pronoun test: somebody is looking into it. Does somebody is looking it into sound possible? No.
3. So look into is inseparable, and the object always follows the whole verb.
That test takes a second and it decides the question without needing a list.
grammar.mistake: Put off it, deal it with, look it into — a pronoun in the wrong position. The pronoun test catches all of them. The other error is register: using sort out and deal with in a formal complaint where resolve and address belong, or writing an entire report in one-word Latin verbs so that it reads as stiff and evasive.
grammar.tip: You know the meanings already. Test the position with a pronoun.
grammar.practice:
Give the formal equivalent, then rewrite with a pronoun object.
1. They put off the meeting.
2. Somebody is looking into the problem.
3. We carried out the inspection.
4. She brought up the cost.
5. They called off the visit.
6. Who deals with complaints?
grammar.answers:
1. postpone — They put it off. (separable)
2. investigate — Somebody is looking into it. (inseparable)
3. perform — We carried it out. (separable)
4. raise — She brought it up. (separable)
5. cancel — They called it off. (separable)
6. handle — Who deals with them? (inseparable)
Four of the six are separable and take the pronoun in the middle. Two — look into and deal with — are inseparable and keep it after.
There is no way to tell from looking at them, which is why the pronoun test is the practical answer rather than a list.
All six formal equivalents are words you already knew. That is the point of the card.

grammar.title: Adjective plus infinitive
grammar.explanation: A small, very useful group of adjectives that take to plus the verb, and two structures built on them that appear constantly.
grammar.rule:
ADJECTIVE + TO + VERB
  I am reluctant to agree.
  She is eager to start.
  They are likely to refuse.
  He is bound to notice.
  I am liable to forget.
  It is prone to fail.

THE GROUP
  reluctant, eager, keen, willing,
  likely, unlikely, bound, liable,
  prone, ready, able, glad, sorry,
  easy, difficult, important

IT IS + ADJECTIVE + TO
  It is difficult to explain.
  It is important to check.
  It is easy to say.
  ^ how English makes a general statement
    about an activity.

  Compare: Explaining it is difficult.
  Both correct. It is... is more common.

TOO and ENOUGH + INFINITIVE
  It is too late to change it.
     too goes BEFORE the adjective
  It is not clear enough to act on.
     enough goes AFTER the adjective

  (from Level 1 Unit 8)
grammar.workedExample:
You want to say that something is hard to put into words.
1. You could use an -ing subject: Explaining it is difficult. That is correct.
2. But English much more often uses the it is structure for general statements about activities.
3. Build it: it is, then the adjective, then to plus the verb.
4. Result: It is difficult to explain.
Now one with too. You want to say the deadline has passed and nothing can be done.
1. Too goes before the adjective: too late.
2. Then to plus the verb: to change it.
3. Result: It is too late to change it.
And one with enough. You want to say a report is not specific enough to act on.
1. Enough goes after the adjective: clear enough.
2. Result: It is not clear enough to act on.
The positions are fixed and opposite — too before, enough after — and that is the only thing on this card that is easy to get wrong.
grammar.mistake: Putting enough before the adjective — enough clear to act on. Too comes before and enough comes after, and they are opposite. The other error is following one of these adjectives with -ing: I am reluctant agreeing, she is eager starting. This group takes to, and prone is the one that takes both — prone to fail and prone to flooding are both correct.
grammar.tip: This group takes to. Too before the adjective, enough after it.
grammar.practice:
Write the sentence.
1. You are unwilling to agree without seeing it.
2. She is very keen to start.
3. Somebody will certainly notice.
4. You often forget unless reminded.
5. Say that explaining something is hard, using it is.
6. Say the deadline has passed, using too.
7. Say a report is not specific enough to act on.
8. Say that bay floods often, using prone.
grammar.answers:
1. I am reluctant to agree without seeing it.
2. She is eager to start.
3. Somebody is bound to notice.
4. I am liable to forget unless somebody reminds me.
5. It is difficult to explain.
6. It is too late to change it.
7. It is not clear enough to act on.
8. That bay is prone to flooding.
Numbers 6 and 7 show the two positions: too before the adjective, enough after it.
Number 8 uses prone with an -ing form rather than an infinitive, which is one of the few adjectives in this group that allows both. Prone to fail is equally correct.
Number 5 could also be Explaining it is difficult, using an -ing subject from card 2. Both are correct and the it is version is much more common.

speaking.title: Speaking 1 — The four that reverse
speaking.instructions:
Say all eight sentences aloud, in pairs, five times.
I remembered to lock it. / I remember locking it.
I stopped to read it. / I stopped reading it.
I tried to open it. / I tried opening it.
I regret to tell you. / I regret telling you.
After each pair, say aloud what the difference is.
Record one full set.
These four repay being learned as pairs, because it is the contrast that makes each one stick.
speaking.tutor: Say four sentences using these verbs and ask the tutor to describe what happened in each.

speaking.title: Speaking 2 — Activities as subjects
speaking.instructions:
Say ten sentences that begin with an -ing form as the subject.
Waiting is the worst part. Explaining it takes longer than doing it.
Make at least three of them long, with a plural noun inside the phrase — checking every pallet before it goes out is slow.
Record all ten.
Play back and check every verb is singular. The long ones with a plural noun near the verb are where the error happens.
speaking.tutor: Say ten -ing subjects and ask the tutor to flag any verb that should be singular.

speaking.title: Speaking 3 — Twelve phrasal verbs
speaking.instructions:
Take twelve phrasal verbs from this unit.
For each, say a true sentence about your own week, then say the formal one-word equivalent.
We put the meeting off. Postpone.
Record all twenty-four.
Then say each one again with a pronoun object and check the position. Put it off, look into it — one splits and one does not.
speaking.tutor: Say twelve phrasal verbs and ask the tutor for the formal equivalent of each.

speaking.title: Speaking 4 — The pronoun test
speaking.instructions:
Take ten phrasal verbs.
For each, say it twice with a pronoun object — once split and once not.
Put it off. Put off it.
Look into it. Look it into.
Record all twenty.
One of each pair will sound impossible. That is the test, and it decides separable from inseparable without needing a list.
speaking.tutor: Ask the tutor to name ten phrasal verbs and say which ones can be split.

speaking.title: Speaking 5 — Two registers
speaking.instructions:
Take a short message you might send at work — three or four sentences.
Say it twice: once in the formal register with one-word verbs, once in ordinary speech with phrasal verbs.
Do this with three different messages.
Record all six.
Listen back and ask which version you would rather receive. Then ask whether the formal one was more precise anywhere — sometimes it genuinely is, and noticing where is the harder half.
speaking.tutor: Say a formal message to the tutor and ask it to say the same thing as a colleague would.

speaking.title: Speaking 6 — Read both versions aloud
speaking.instructions:
Open Reading 3.
Read the original note aloud, then the supervisor's version.
Then say aloud: four phrasal verbs in the second and the formal equivalent each replaced.
Then say what regrets to advise means, and why it is to rather than -ing.
Then say whether anything in the original was genuinely more precise.
Record the last three parts and keep them.
speaking.tutor: Read the tutor the original note and ask it to explain in plain English what staff are being asked to do.

writing.title: Writing 1 — Twenty verb patterns
writing.prompt:
Write twenty true sentences about your own work, study or life.
Eight must use a verb followed by to.
Eight must use a verb followed by -ing.
Four must use one of the four verbs that take both — remember, stop, try, regret — and for each, write a second sentence using the other pattern and one line saying what changed.
At least three sentences must have an -ing form as the subject, with a singular verb.
writing.model:
1. I intend to ask about the training before the end of the month.
2. I hope to finish the backlog this week.
3. We aim to reply within two working days.
4. She refused to sign it without a date.
5. I tend to check the figures twice.
6. Nobody offered to help.
7. He failed to mention the cost.
8. She deserves to be told first.
9. I enjoy working with people who ask questions.
10. I avoid promising anything on a Friday.
11. She recommended reading it twice.
12. I risk losing an hour every time I do not check.
13. He kept saying it was fine.
14. I have finished checking the sheets.
15. I resent being asked twice.
16. Nobody minds waiting if they are told why.
17. Waiting is the worst part of the whole process.
18. Explaining the system takes longer than using it.
19. Checking every pallet before it goes out is slow but it works.
20. Not being told was the real problem.

Both-verbs:
I remembered to lock the office. / I remember locking the office. — First: I did it. Second: I have the memory of doing it.
I stopped to read the notice. / I stopped reading the notice. — First: I started reading. Second: I finished.
I tried to open it. / I tried opening it. — First: I attempted it and probably failed. Second: I opened it to see whether that helped.
I regret to say it has been cancelled. / I regret saying it was fine. — First: giving bad news now. Second: I wish I had not said it.
writing.length: Twenty sentences plus four both-verb pairs
writing.criteria: Eight verbs taking to and eight taking -ing, all correct; three -ing subjects with singular verbs; four both-verb pairs each with a one-line explanation of the difference; every sentence true about the writer
writing.support: Write the -ing group first. Learners over-produce infinitives because to feels like the default, so starting with -ing forces the other half of the vocabulary out.
writing.extension: Find any sentence where you were not sure which pattern the verb takes. Those are the verbs to look up — and there will be some, because there is no rule.

writing.title: Writing 2 — One message, two registers
writing.prompt:
Write a short work message of five or six sentences — announcing a change, reporting a problem, or asking people to do something.
Write it twice.
Version A: formal, using one-word verbs throughout — postpone, investigate, establish, cancel, resolve, indicate, encounter.
Version B: ordinary, using the phrasal equivalents.
Then write three lines: which you would actually send, whether Version A was more precise anywhere, and which version took longer to write.
writing.model:
VERSION A
Following the failure of the second conveyor, management has resolved to postpone the stock count until the fault has been investigated. An inspection will be performed on Thursday. Personnel encountering any further faults should indicate them to a supervisor immediately. The overtime scheduled for Saturday has been cancelled. An alternative date will be established once the inspection has concluded.

VERSION B
The second conveyor has gone again, so we're putting the stock count off until somebody has looked into it. There'll be an inspection on Thursday. If you come across any more faults, point them out to a supervisor straight away. Saturday's overtime has been called off — sorry. We'll set up another date once the inspection is done.

1. I would send Version B. It says everything A says and people would read it.
2. A is more precise in one place: personnel encountering any further faults is tighter than if you come across any more faults, because it does not depend on who is being addressed. Everything else in A is longer without being clearer.
3. A took longer to write, which surprised me. Reaching for the formal verb every time is slower than saying what happened.
writing.length: Two versions of five or six sentences plus three lines
writing.criteria: Both versions carry the same information; Version A uses at least five one-word verbs; Version B uses the phrasal equivalent of each; three lines including an honest judgement about where A was more precise
writing.support: Write Version B first, in the words you would actually use, then convert it upward. Converting downward from a formal draft tends to leave formal residue in the ordinary version.
writing.extension: Give Version A to somebody and ask them to tell you what they are being asked to do. Then give them B.

writing.title: Writing 3 — Read the note and the rewrite
writing.prompt:
Use the note and the rewrite in Reading 3. Write full-sentence answers.
1. Find five phrasal verbs in the supervisor's version and give the formal word each replaced.
2. The original says management regrets to advise. What does regret plus to mean, and how would regret plus -ing differ?
3. Which version is clearer, and does clearer mean less professional? Explain.
4. Is anything in the original genuinely more precise than the rewrite?
5. Rewrite the original's third paragraph so it is both precise and readable.
writing.model:
1. Putting off replaced postpone. Looked into replaced investigation. Come across replaced encountered. Point out replaced indicated. Called off replaced cancelled. Set up replaced scheduled.
2. Regret plus to means the writer is about to give bad news and is sorry to be giving it. Regret plus -ing would mean they wished they had not given it — management regrets advising you would be an admission that telling staff was a mistake.
3. The supervisor's version is clearer, and it is not less professional. It contains every instruction the original contains, and it was written because the original had not been understood. A document that fails to communicate has failed at its only job, whatever register it is in.
4. Yes, in two places. Pending the outcome is tighter than until we know more, because it names what is being waited for. And the week commencing 21 March is unambiguous where the week of the 21st could be read two ways.
5. Model: If you come across anything unusual, tell a supervisor the same day — please do not wait until the end of the week.
That keeps come across and tell, which are readable, and replaces without delay with a specific deadline, which is more precise than either original.
writing.criteria: Five phrasal verbs correctly paired with their formal equivalents; answer 2 explains both patterns; answer 3 judges by whether the document worked; answer 4 identifies at least one genuine gain in the original; answer 5 produces a version that is both readable and more precise than either
writing.support: Read the two documents side by side, paragraph against paragraph. They are ordered identically, so every formal verb has its phrasal twin a few lines below it.
writing.extension: Count the words in each version. The formal one is longer and says nothing extra, which is worth noticing.

writing.title: Writing 4 — Correct the twelve
writing.prompt:
Every sentence has exactly one mistake from this unit.
Write each out correctly and say which pattern it came from.
1. I am interested in to work here.
2. I enjoy to work with people who ask questions.
3. I intend asking before Friday.
4. I stopped reading the notice. (you were walking, then read it)
5. I remember to lock the door. (you have the memory of doing it)
6. I regret telling you that it has been cancelled. (this is a formal bad-news opening)
7. Waiting are the worst part.
8. Checking every pallet before it goes out are slow.
9. Being not told was the problem.
10. We put off it until Friday.
11. Somebody is looking it into.
12. It is not enough clear to act on.
writing.model:
1. I am interested in working here. (Pattern 1 — after a preposition, always -ing)
2. I enjoy working with people who ask questions. (Pattern 1 — enjoy takes -ing)
3. I intend to ask before Friday. (Pattern 1 — intend is a future verb and takes to)
4. I stopped to read the notice. (Pattern 1 — you stopped in order to read)
5. I remember locking the door. (Pattern 1 — a memory takes -ing)
6. I regret to tell you that it has been cancelled. (Pattern 1 — bad news about to be given takes to)
7. Waiting is the worst part. (Pattern 2 — an -ing subject is singular)
8. Checking every pallet before it goes out is slow. (Pattern 2 — the subject is the activity, not the pallets)
9. Not being told was the problem. (Pattern 2 — the negative goes before the -ing form)
10. We put it off until Friday. (Pattern 3 — a pronoun goes in the middle of a separable verb)
11. Somebody is looking into it. (Pattern 3 — look into is inseparable)
12. It is not clear enough to act on. (Pattern 4 — enough goes after the adjective)
writing.criteria: All twelve corrected; each labelled with the right pattern; numbers 4, 5 and 6 corrected by meaning rather than by rule; numbers 10 and 11 corrected in opposite directions
writing.support: Numbers 10 and 11 are the pronoun test twice, in opposite directions. Say each aloud both ways and one will sound impossible — that is the answer.
writing.extension: Numbers 4, 5 and 6 were all grammatical sentences that meant the wrong thing. Write one more of each.

activities.title: Practice 1 — To or -ing
activities.instructions:
Write to plus the verb or the -ing form.
1. I intend ____ (ask) before Friday.
2. I enjoy ____ (work) here.
3. I am interested in ____ (work) here.
4. She refused ____ (sign) it.
5. I avoid ____ (promise) anything on a Friday.
6. We aim ____ (reply) within two days.
7. He kept ____ (say) it was fine.
8. I have finished ____ (check) the sheets.
9. She recommended ____ (read) it twice.
10. Instead of ____ (wait), I went home.
11. I tend ____ (check) twice.
12. Nobody minds ____ (wait) if they are told why.
activities.answers:
1. to ask  2. working  3. working  4. to sign  5. promising  6. to reply  7. saying  8. checking  9. reading  10. waiting  11. to check  12. waiting
The to group — 1, 4, 6, 11 — are all future or intention verbs. The -ing group — 2, 5, 7, 8, 9, 12 — are all liking, avoiding or continuing verbs.
Numbers 3 and 10 are the absolute rule: after in and after instead of, only -ing is possible.
Number 9 is worth checking. Recommend never takes to — recommend to read is a very common error.

activities.title: Practice 2 — The four that take both
activities.instructions:
Write the sentence that matches the meaning in brackets.
1. remember / lock the door (you did it)
2. remember / lock the door (you have the memory)
3. stop / read the notice (you were walking, then read it)
4. stop / read the notice (you were reading, then stopped)
5. try / open it (you attempted it and failed)
6. try / open it (you opened it as an experiment)
7. regret / tell you (you are about to give bad news)
8. regret / tell you (you wish you had not)
9. remember / send the invoice (a task you must not forget)
10. remember / send the invoice (you are sure you sent it)
11. try / restart it (an experiment to see if it helps)
12. stop / check the figures (you were doing something else, then checked)
activities.answers:
1. I remembered to lock the door.
2. I remember locking the door.
3. I stopped to read the notice.
4. I stopped reading the notice.
5. I tried to open it.
6. I tried opening it.
7. I regret to tell you.
8. I regret telling you.
9. Remember to send the invoice.
10. I remember sending the invoice.
11. I tried restarting it.
12. I stopped to check the figures.
Every odd-numbered item takes to and every even one takes -ing, except 9 to 12 which mix.
The pattern across all four verbs: to points forward to a task or an intention; -ing points back to something that already happened or is already under way.
Numbers 3 and 4 remain the clearest pair. In 3 the reading starts; in 4 it stops.

activities.title: Practice 3 — Phrasal verbs and their formal twins
activities.instructions:
Give the formal one-word equivalent, then rewrite the sentence with a pronoun object.
1. They put off the meeting.
2. Somebody is looking into the problem.
3. We carried out the inspection.
4. She brought up the cost.
5. They called off the visit.
6. Who deals with complaints?
7. They set up a new system.
8. We sorted out the paperwork.
9. I came across two errors.
10. She pointed out the mistake.
11. We took on two new staff.
12. We ran out of the smaller size.
13. He looked after the equipment.
14. I looked up the reference.
15. They put the meeting off again.
16. Nobody has looked into it.
activities.answers:
1. postpone — They put it off. SEPARABLE
2. investigate — Somebody is looking into it. INSEPARABLE
3. perform — We carried it out. SEPARABLE
4. raise — She brought it up. SEPARABLE
5. cancel — They called it off. SEPARABLE
6. handle — Who deals with them? INSEPARABLE
7. establish — They set it up. SEPARABLE
8. resolve — We sorted it out. SEPARABLE
9. encounter — I came across them. INSEPARABLE
10. indicate — She pointed it out. SEPARABLE
11. recruit — We took them on. SEPARABLE
12. exhaust — We ran out of it. INSEPARABLE
13. maintain — He looked after it. INSEPARABLE
14. consult — I looked it up. SEPARABLE
15. postpone — They put it off again. SEPARABLE
16. investigate — Nobody has looked into it. INSEPARABLE
The inseparable ones here are look into, deal with, come across, run out of and look after. Nothing about their form predicts this, which is why the pronoun test exists.
Compare 13 and 14: look after is inseparable and look up is separable, and they look identical.
Every formal equivalent in this list is a word you already knew before this unit.

activities.title: Practice 4 — Adjective plus infinitive
activities.instructions:
Write the sentence.
1. You are unwilling to agree without seeing it.
2. She is very keen to start.
3. Somebody will certainly notice.
4. You often forget unless reminded.
5. That bay floods often. Use prone.
6. The old machines often fail. Use liable.
7. Explaining something is hard. Use it is.
8. Checking is important. Use it is.
9. The deadline has passed. Use too.
10. The report is not specific enough for action. Use enough.
11. It is not obvious how to do it. Use easy.
12. They will probably refuse. Use likely.
activities.answers:
1. I am reluctant to agree without seeing it.
2. She is eager to start.
3. Somebody is bound to notice.
4. I am liable to forget unless somebody reminds me.
5. That bay is prone to flooding.
6. The old machines are liable to fail.
7. It is difficult to explain.
8. It is important to check.
9. It is too late to change it.
10. It is not clear enough to act on.
11. It is not easy to do.
12. They are likely to refuse.
Numbers 9 and 10 show the two fixed positions: too before the adjective, enough after it. They are opposite and both are easy to reverse.
Number 5 uses prone with an -ing form and number 6 uses liable with an infinitive. Prone accepts both; most of this group takes only the infinitive.
Numbers 7, 8, 9, 10 and 11 all use the it is structure, which is how English makes a general statement about an activity.

activities.title: Practice 5 — Collect twenty verb patterns
activities.instructions:
This week, collect twenty verbs from real English, each with what follows it.
Write each one down inside the phrase you found it in, not on its own.
Sort them into to, -ing, and both.
Mark any that surprised you.
Then check three of your uncertain ones in a dictionary.
activities.answers:
No key — they are your verbs.
What most people find: the tendencies hold for perhaps two thirds of what they collect. Future and intention verbs take to; liking, avoiding and continuing verbs take -ing. The remaining third simply has to be learned, and that is the honest proportion.
The second finding is about the preposition rule. Every single -ing form following a preposition will be correct, without exception, and that is worth confirming from real data rather than taking on trust.
The third finding is that writing each verb inside a phrase makes a large difference later. Recommend plus -ing learned as a rule is one fact; she recommended reading it twice learned as a sentence is something you can reuse without reconstructing it.

activities.title: Practice 6 — Translate a formal document downward
activities.instructions:
Find a real formal document — a policy, a notice, an official letter, terms of service.
Copy out six sentences that use one-word Latin verbs.
Rewrite each with a phrasal verb.
Then mark any where the formal version was genuinely more precise, and say why.
Write one line on whether the document would be better in the plain version.
activities.answers:
No key — it is your document.
What most people find: most of the formal verbs translate down with no loss at all. Postpone, investigate, establish, cancel, resolve, indicate and encounter all have exact phrasal equivalents, and the plain version is shorter.
The second finding is the important one, and it stops this becoming a rule that formal writing is always worse. Some formal verbs are genuinely more precise, usually because they carry a narrower meaning — ascertain is not quite find out, and terminate is not quite end. Where you find one of those, the formal word is earning its place.
The third finding: documents are rarely improved by being translated entirely into one register. The best version usually keeps the precise formal words and replaces the rest, which is what the supervisor's note in Reading 3 does not quite manage and what Writing 3 question 5 asks you to do.

options: I am interested in working here.
I am interested to working here.
I am interested in to work here.
I am interested in work here.
quizzes.a: I am interested in working here.
quizzes.why: Anything after a preposition takes -ing. This is the one rule in the area with no exceptions at all.

quizzes.q: I remembered to lock the door. What does this mean?
options: You have a memory of locking it
You remembered, and then you locked it
You forgot to lock it
You are about to lock it
quizzes.a: You remembered, and then you locked it
quizzes.why: Remember plus to points forward to a task. Remember plus -ing points back to a memory you hold.

quizzes.q: I stopped reading the notice. What happened?
options: You stopped in order to read it
You never read it
You were reading and you stopped
You read it twice
quizzes.a: You were reading and you stopped
quizzes.why: I stopped to read the notice would mean the opposite — you stopped doing something else in order to start reading.

options: Waiting are the worst part.
Wait is the worst part.
To waiting is the worst part.
Waiting is the worst part.
quizzes.why: An -ing subject is singular, because the whole phrase names one activity. This holds even when a plural noun sits inside the phrase.

options: Checking every pallet before it goes out is slow.
Checking every pallet before it goes out are slow.
Check every pallet before it goes out is slow.
To checking every pallet is slow.
quizzes.a: Checking every pallet before it goes out is slow.
quizzes.why: The subject is the activity, not the pallets. The plural noun sitting next to the verb is exactly what makes this error tempting.

quizzes.q: What is the formal equivalent of look into?
options: establish
investigate
postpone
encounter
quizzes.why: Almost every common phrasal verb has a one-word formal twin, and the formal one is usually the version learners already know.

options: We put off it until Friday.
We off put it until Friday.
We put it off until Friday.
We put off until Friday it.
quizzes.a: We put it off until Friday.
quizzes.why: Put off is separable, and with a separable verb a pronoun object must go in the middle.

options: Somebody is looking it into.
Somebody is looking it in.
Somebody is into looking it.
Somebody is looking into it.
quizzes.why: Look into is inseparable, so the object stays after the whole verb. The pronoun test is what tells you which kind you have.

options: One-word verbs in formal writing, phrasal verbs in speech
Phrasal verbs in formal writing, one-word verbs in speech
Both are the same
Phrasal verbs should always be avoided
quizzes.a: One-word verbs in formal writing, phrasal verbs in speech
quizzes.why: A document written entirely in one-word Latin verbs reads as stiff and slightly evasive, and sort out in a formal complaint sounds casual where resolve would not.

options: It is not enough clear to act on.
It is not clear enough to act on.
It is too clear enough to act on.
It is enough not clear to act on.
quizzes.a: It is not clear enough to act on.
quizzes.why: Enough goes after the adjective and too goes before it. The two positions are fixed and opposite.

quizzes.q: Which adjective is followed by an infinitive?
options: good
interested
reluctant
keen on
quizzes.why: Reluctant to agree. Interested, good and keen on all take a preposition, and anything after a preposition takes -ing.

quizzes.q: Management regrets to advise. What does this mean?
options: They wish they had not told you
They will advise later
They advised somebody by mistake
They are about to give bad news and are sorry
quizzes.a: They are about to give bad news and are sorry
quizzes.why: Regret plus to is the formal bad-news opening. Regret plus -ing would mean they wished they had not said it.

teacherNotes.note: Four pattern cards, each with a worked example, and every exercise has an answer key or an explicit no-key note with a what-most-people-find finding. Practice 2 is the diagnostic and it supplies the intended meaning in brackets for every item, so the learner must reason from meaning to form rather than pattern-matching.

teacherNotes.type: Say plainly that there is no rule
teacherNotes.note: Which verbs take to and which take -ing has to be learned verb by verb, exactly like the adjective-preposition pairings in Unit 1 of this level. Learners lose real time searching for a system. What the card gives instead is three tendencies for guessing and one absolute rule — anything after a preposition takes -ing — and separating the reliable from the arbitrary is more useful than presenting both as patterns.

teacherNotes.type: The four both-verbs are worth disproportionate time
teacherNotes.note: Remember, stop, try and regret produce sentences that mean the opposite of what was intended, which no other error in this unit does. They should be learned as pairs rather than individually, because the contrast is what makes each stick. Speaking 1 drills all eight sentences together for this reason, and Writing 4 numbers 4, 5 and 6 are all grammatical sentences meaning the wrong thing.

teacherNotes.type: Reframe phrasal verbs as a register problem
teacherNotes.note: Learners believe they are missing thousands of meanings. They are not — they know investigate, postpone, establish and cancel already, and they are missing the versions people say. Reading 2 makes this explicit and it changes how large the task feels. The register point is equally important in both directions: sort out in a formal complaint is as wrong as endeavour to ascertain in a note to colleagues.

teacherNotes.type: The pronoun test replaces a list
teacherNotes.note: There is no way to tell separable from inseparable by looking, and Practice 3 pairs look after with look up to show that identical-looking verbs behave differently. Trying the verb with a pronoun and hearing which position is impossible resolves most cases in a second, and it works on verbs the learner has never met.

teacherNotes.type: Do not let the register point become an anti-formality rule
teacherNotes.note: Reading 3's comprehension deliberately asks whether anything in the original was genuinely more precise, and the answer is yes — pending the outcome and the week commencing are both tighter than their plain replacements. Practice 6's key makes the same point about ascertain and terminate. The best version of a document usually keeps the precise formal words and replaces the rest.

The AI tutor is a rehearsal partner and no task here is scored by it alone. Writing 2 asks for a real work message and Practice 6 sends learners to a real formal document, which may be their own tenancy agreement, employment contract or a letter about their circumstances. No sentence from a document about the learner's own situation, and no employer or colleague name, should be collected, shared or entered into the app. Writing 3 works from the note supplied in Reading 3, and that framing should stay.

selfAssessment.statement: I can tell what changes between I stopped to read it and I stopped reading it.
I can say waiting is the worst part, and keep the verb singular.
I can say look into rather than investigate, and put it off rather than put off it.
I can say it is difficult to explain and too late to change it.

assignment.title: Verb patterns collected, and one message in two registers
assignment.instructions: Two parts. First, record the eight sentences of the four both-verbs in pairs, saying after each pair what the difference is; then record twelve phrasal verbs in true sentences about your own week, giving the formal equivalent of each and testing the pronoun position. Second, write the twenty sentences from Writing 1 with the four both-verb pairs and their explanations, write one work message in both registers as directed in Writing 2 with the three lines of commentary, and add your full-sentence answers to the five questions in Writing 3 including the rewritten paragraph. Keep everything together.
assignment.submissionType: An audio recording and written work
